# Tree-based structures (Octree, Pointer Tree, Sparse Voxel DAG)

Also called: Sparse Voxel Trees, Hierarchical Voxel Structures, Tree-based Sparse Volumes

## Overview
Tree-based structures represent sparse volumetric data by recursively subdividing the 3D domain into hierarchical nodes, storing data only for occupied regions to achieve [compression](#4-compression.md) proportional to sparsity [S1, S2, S3]. They solve the memory bottleneck of dense voxel grids by enabling efficient culling of empty space during rendering or query operations. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like [Hash Grids](#936-hash-grids.md) (flat, no hierarchy) and Brick Maps (fixed-size blocks) is the variable depth and branching factor, which allows adaptive resolution and precise spatial locality management [S1, S2, S3].

## Shared principles
All structures in this family share the following mechanism:

1.  **[Recursive Subdivision](#1304-recursive-subdivision.md):** The 3D domain is recursively divided into sub-volumes. In standard octrees, each node has 8 children. In pointer trees, the branching factor $N$ varies ($N^3$ children).
2.  **Sparsity Encoding:** Empty regions are represented by null pointers or absence of children, rather than storing zero-valued voxels. This provides compression proportional to the sparsity of the data.
3.  **[Hierarchical Traversal](#896-hierarchical-traversal.md):** Rendering or access requires traversing from the root to the leaf. This allows skipping large empty volumes (culling) and adapting resolution to view distance or detail requirements.
4.  **Spatial Locality:** Children of a node are spatially contiguous. This locality is often exploited via Morton ordering (Z-order curve) to map 3D coordinates to 1D keys, enabling efficient neighbor lookups and linear array representations in implicit variants [G].
5.  **Subtree Merging:** The core differentiator of the DAG family is the identification of structurally identical subtrees (isomorphic nodes) and their replacement with a single shared instance. This transforms the tree topology into a graph where multiple parents may reference the same child node, eliminating redundancy [S1, S2].

## Subtopics

### [Compact pointer tree](844-compact-pointer-tree.md)
Uses variable branching factor $N$ ($2 \le N \le 6$) and 8-bit relative pointers to optimize memory for terabyte-scale [RGBA](#5142-color-packing-rgba.md) data, enabling real-time rendering via hierarchical DDA.

### [Sparse Voxel DAGs](2791-sparse-voxel-dags.md)
Merges identical subtrees into shared nodes to reduce memory footprint by 1–3 orders of magnitude compared to standard SVOs, explicitly decoupling geometry from material attributes.

### [Octree-based structures](2792-octree-based-structures.md)
Uses a fixed 8-way branching factor, offering a trade-off between pointer overhead, traversal depth, and spatial locality management.

### [Span Space Tree](4379-span-space-tree.md)
Embeds axis-aligned span intervals within the hierarchy to reduce visited cells during traversal, refining interval trees for large-scale volumes.

### [Sparse Voxel Tree (SVO Tree)](4983-sparse-voxel-tree-svo-tree.md)
A standard hierarchical structure with fixed 8 children per node, allocating memory only for non-empty regions, providing compression proportional to sparsity.

### [Tiny LOD](6968-tiny-lod.md)
Constructs a hierarchical LOD tree from splat data with explicit merge filtering, outputting encoded opacity and [chunk trees](#4050-chunk-trees.md).

### [NerfTree](7559-nerftree.md)
A two-level sparse voxel structure for NeRFs, decoupling coarse geometry caching from fine radiance refinement to accelerate training and inference.

### [Adaptively Sampled Distance Fields](7773-adaptively-sampled-distance-fields.md)
Compresses SDFs using tree simplification with sign preservation to maintain zero-isosurface topology, suitable for resolution-independent [antialiasing](#4802-antialiasing-aa.md).

## Background
Tree-based [sparse structures](#5-sparse-structures.md) originated in the early 1990s as a solution to the memory inefficiency of dense voxel grids in volume rendering and geometric modeling [G]. The [Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO)](#8749-sparse-voxel-octree-svo.md) was popularized in the mid-2000s for real-time ray tracing and volume visualization, enabling the rendering of large datasets by skipping empty space [S2, S3]. Subsequent developments introduced DAGs to handle geometric redundancy [S1, S2], compact pointer trees for GPU-friendly terabyte-scale data [S1, S2], and adaptations for neural rendering ([NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)) and distance fields [S1, S2, S3]. These structures are now standard in high-performance volume rendering, medical imaging, and geometric compression.
